summary: Discusses how TLS and IPsec can secure SIGTRAN protocols and recommends the minimum security a node must implement. IPsec support is mandatory and TLS is optional.

eli5.summary: Phone signals carried over the internet need protection. This says every device must support a strong lock, and may support a second kind.

subtitle: Which security the signaling-over-IP protocols must support: IPsec is mandatory, TLS is optional.

tldr.problem: SIGTRAN protocols carry telephony signaling over IP, where the traditional closed-network protection of telephony no longer applies.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC explains how IPsec and TLS can protect SIGTRAN traffic running over SCTP, and sets rules for each, including a STARTTLS upgrade procedure for TLS.
tldr.outcome: A SIGTRAN node MUST support IPsec and MAY support TLS. Peers should use the same mechanism across all their sessions.

today: RFC 3788 is a Proposed Standard, published in June 2004. No later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The SIGTRAN protocols carry signaling messages for telephony services. IUA is used between customer premise and service provider equipment. M2UA, M2PA, M3UA and SUA are used between service provider equipment only.

The security needs differ between these situations and involve several parties: end-users, service providers and the applications involved. Local regulation may add more. The SIGTRAN protocols assume messages are secured by IPsec or TLS, and this RFC recommends the minimum security a SIGTRAN node must implement.
sections.eli5: These protocols carry the signals that set up phone calls. Different groups care about keeping them safe, so there have to be shared rules.

sections.title: Security in Telephony Networks
sections.content:
Telephony security mostly rests on the closed network principle. SS7 networks are often physically remote or inaccessible and equipment is often under lock and key. Packet filtering is sometimes used at boundaries between SS7 networks, and end-users are not directly connected to SS7 networks.

Access protocols such as ISDN carry end-user signaling, and telephone switches run by operators translate it to SS7-based protocols. The RFC notes there are no standardized ways of using encryption for confidentiality or technologies for authentication in these networks.
sections.eli5: Old phone networks stayed safe by being locked away in buildings. Once signals travel over the internet, a locked door is not enough.

sections.title: Threats and Goals
sections.content:
The RFC separates passive attacks, where an attacker reads packets but does not write them, from active attacks, where the attacker also writes data, such as replay, message insertion, deletion or modification, and man-in-the-middle attacks.

The general objectives are communication security (peer authentication, integrity, confidentiality, replay protection), non-repudiation, and system security (avoiding unauthorized use, inappropriate use and denial of service).

All SIGTRAN protocols use SCTP as transport, which resists blind denial of service attacks such as flooding, masquerade and improper monopolization of services. The RFC states that there is no one-size-fits-all solution and that end-to-end security should be the goal, using IPsec or TLS to protect the confidentiality of user payload.
sections.eli5: Some attackers only listen, and some also change or fake messages. The aim is to stop both kinds.

sections.title: IPsec Usage
sections.content:
Nodes using IPsec MUST implement ESP in transport mode with non-null encryption and authentication algorithms, and MUST implement IPsec's replay protection. ESP in tunnel mode SHOULD be used where IP layer protection is needed.

All SIGTRAN nodes MUST support IKE for peer authentication, security association negotiation and key management. Pre-shared key authentication MUST be supported; certificate-based authentication with digital signatures MAY be. With pre-shared keys in transport mode, IKE Aggressive Mode SHOULD be used and Main Mode SHOULD NOT.

Phase 2 Quick Mode exchanges MUST carry the Identity Payloads, each with a single IP address and a single non-zero port number, so a security association maps to specific TCP and SCTP connections. Receiving a Phase 2 delete message SHOULD NOT cause a SIGTRAN session to be torn down.

Because SCTP supports multi-homed hosts, implementations SHOULD support the IPsec feature described in RFC 3554, which addresses the need for multiple security associations.
sections.eli5: The first lock wraps every packet in a sealed envelope and checks who is on the other end. Nodes must be ready to use a shared secret password for that check.

sections.title: TLS Usage
sections.content:
The node that starts an SCTP association acts as TLS client and the accepting node acts as TLS server. Peers using TLS MUST mutually authenticate. The cipher suite TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA is required by RFC 3436, and other suites MAY be negotiated. TLS MUST be used on all bi-directional streams, and uni-directional streams MUST NOT be used. SCTP unordered delivery cannot be used with TLS.

Because TLS protects only the payload, the SCTP header and control chunks are not protected, which can be used for DoS attacks.

SIGTRAN uses the same SCTP port number and payload protocol identifier when run over TLS, so a session upgrade is used. An ASP configured for TLS sends STARTTLS on stream 0, starts timer T_TLS, and sends nothing else until TLS is established. A peer without TLS replies with an ERROR message and the association is terminated. A peer with TLS replies STARTTLS_ACK, and the client starts TLS. If the timer expires, the association is terminated. Both messages are a common header only, with message types 1 and 2.

A man-in-the-middle could cause a denial of service by claiming the peer does not support TLS, but such an attack is always possible for a man-in-the-middle.
sections.eli5: The second lock is asked for politely. One side says "can we use TLS?", the other says yes or no, and if there is no answer in time they hang up.

sections.title: Choosing Between IPsec and TLS
sections.content:
With IPsec ESP, SCTP control information is encrypted and protected. With TLS it is not encrypted and is protected only by SCTP procedures. In both cases the IP header is neither encrypted nor protected. Since both have enough mechanisms, the recommendation is: a SIGTRAN node MUST support IPsec and MAY support TLS.

For peer-to-peer use (M2PA, M3UA and SUA), trust configuration is essential. IPsec is less flexible than TLS about trust anchors because ports cannot be used in IKE Phase 1, so one policy covers all applications. Pre-shared keys require the peers to be known beforehand.

Peers are recommended to use the same mechanism across all sessions, since inconsistency can mean redundant mechanisms such as TLS over IPsec, or potential vulnerabilities. A simple static policy is suggested: initiate IPsec for outbound traffic to destination port P, and require it for inbound traffic.
sections.eli5: Both locks work. The rule is that every device must have the first kind, may also have the second, and should keep using the same kind with all its friends.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says message class 12 has been reserved in the Signaling User Adaption Layer Assignments Registry, with message type 1 reserved for STARTTLS and type 2 for STARTTLS_ACK. The body of the RFC describes the same messages as message class 10, so the two places disagree.
sections.eli5: The special messages for asking about TLS got their own reserved numbers in an official list.

messages.label: STARTTLS
messages.note: Sent on stream 0; starts timer T_TLS.

messages.label: STARTTLS_ACK
messages.note: Peer supports TLS; TLS-based communication begins.
